title: The Holiness of the Priests
summary: God gives special rules for the priests, Aaron's descendants, who serve at the altar. Ordinary priests may become unclean by contact with the dead only for their closest relatives and must not adopt pagan mourning rites or marry a prostitute or a divorced woman. The high priest may not mourn even for his parents and must marry a virgin of his own people. Priests with physical defects may eat the holy food but may not offer sacrifices or approach the veil.
story: Chapters 18 to 20 set out the holiness required of all Israel. Chapters 21 and 22 narrow the focus to the priests, who live closest to God's presence and so are held to a stricter standard. The logic is one of concentric circles: the camp is holy, the tabernacle holier, the Most Holy Place holiest; so too the people are holy, the priests holier, the high priest holiest. The chapter follows the ordination of Aaron and his sons (Leviticus 8 and 9) and the death of Nadab and Abihu (Leviticus 10), which showed what happens when priests treat holiness lightly.
historical:
Israel's priesthood was hereditary, passed down in the family of Aaron, Moses' brother, from the tribe of Levi. Priests offered sacrifices, taught the law, and judged questions of clean and unclean. The high priest, anointed with sacred oil and dressed in special garments, alone entered the Most Holy Place on the Day of Atonement. As with the rest of Leviticus, traditional readers date these rules to Moses at Sinai, while many critical scholars see them as reflecting the priesthood of the Jerusalem temple in a later period. The rules remained in force for centuries. The prophet Ezekiel, in his vision of a restored temple in the sixth century BC, restates them in a stricter form (Ezekiel 44:20-25), limiting ordinary priests to marrying a virgin of Israel or a priest's widow.

Priests in other ancient Near Eastern religions also served under purity requirements, and some cultures required that those who served in a temple or a royal court be physically without blemish. The book of Daniel reflects a similar expectation at the Babylonian court, where the young men chosen for service were to be without physical defect (Daniel 1:4). Israel's priests were set apart in a comparable way, but their rules were tied to the character of their God rather than the prestige of a king.
cultural:
Contact with a dead body made a person ritually unclean, unfit to approach the sanctuary until purified (Numbers 19). For an ordinary Israelite that was a normal part of life, since families prepared and buried their own dead. For a priest it meant being barred from his work, so the law limits it to the closest relatives: parents, children, a brother, and an unmarried sister who had no husband to bury her. The high priest could not become unclean even for his father or mother, and he could not show the usual signs of grief by letting his hair hang loose or tearing his clothes. The shaving and cutting forbidden in verse 5 were mourning customs among Israel's neighbors, forbidden to all Israel in 19:27-28 and repeated here for priests.

The marriage rules protected the priestly family line and its reputation. A priest's household represented God before the people, so a scandal there profaned more than the family. The harsh sentence for a priest's daughter who became a prostitute (verse 9) reflects that her act disgraced her father's sacred office. The list of physical defects in verses 17 to 23 parallels the requirement that sacrificial animals be without blemish (22:17-25). A priest with a defect was not cut off from the priestly family: he still ate the holy and most holy food (verse 22). He was only barred from officiating at the altar and the veil.
literary: The chapter has two parts, each introduced by God speaking to Moses (verses 1 and 16). The first (verses 1 to 15) addresses ordinary priests and then the high priest, moving from the less strict to the more strict. The second (verses 17 to 23) addresses priests with physical defects. The line "I am the LORD who sanctifies" closes the high priest's rules and the chapter (verses 15 and 23), with a similar statement in verse 8, reminding readers that the priests' holiness comes from God before it is demanded of them. The phrase "the food of their God" (verse 6, repeated in similar form in verses 8, 17, 21, and 22) uses a traditional description of the offerings, not implying that God eats but presenting the altar as his table and the priests as those who serve at it. The final verse notes that Moses spoke these words to all Israel, not only the priests, so the whole people knew what was expected of those who served them.

outline.t: Priests and mourning for the dead
The stricter holiness of the high priest
Moses tells Aaron, his sons, and all Israel

doctrines.note: Holiness increases with closeness to God. Those who serve nearest his presence bear greater restrictions, not as a privilege to boast in but as a weight to carry. God himself is the one who sanctifies them.

The chapter sets a standard for priesthood that no ordinary priest fully met: undefiled, without blemish, wholly given to God's service. The New Testament presents Jesus as the high priest who meets that standard perfectly.

The priest with a physical defect remains a full member of the priestly family and eats the most holy food. The restriction concerns the symbolic role of officiating at the altar, not his worth before God or his place among God's people.

words.note: Chalal, to profane: to make something holy common, to treat it as ordinary. It appears seven times in this chapter. A priest who defiles himself profanes himself and God's name, because the holiness of his office is not his own; it belongs to God and reflects on him.

Mum, blemish or defect. The same word is used for flaws in sacrificial animals (22:20-25). It describes physical wholeness, not moral worth. The idea is that what comes near God's altar, whether priest or offering, should display the wholeness that belongs to God's presence.

Lechem, bread or food. The offerings are called the food of God, a phrase found in several places in Leviticus. It reflects old sacrificial language in which the altar is God's table, though Israel's faith rejected the idea that God needs food (Psalm 50:12-13).

Nezer, consecration, from a root meaning to separate. In verse 12 the anointing oil is the high priest's consecration. The same word describes the high priest's gold plate (Exodus 29:6), a king's crown, and the Nazirite's separated hair (Numbers 6).

christ: The letter to the Hebrews describes Jesus as the high priest this chapter was looking for: "holy, innocent, undefiled, set apart from sinners, and exalted above the heavens" (Hebrews 7:26). Unlike Aaron's descendants, he did not need to offer sacrifices for his own sins first (Hebrews 7:27). Yet the Gospels show a striking reversal. Where the priests had to avoid the dead and the unclean to protect their holiness, Jesus touched a leper and made him clean (Mark 1:41), took a dead girl by the hand, and touched the bier of a widow's son. His holiness was not endangered by contact; it overcame uncleanness. And while men with defects could not serve at the altar, the Gospels record that "The blind and the lame came to Him at the temple, and He healed them" (Matthew 21:14), and Jesus told his followers to invite "the poor, the crippled, the lame, and the blind" to their banquets (Luke 14:13). The New Testament also calls all believers "a holy priesthood" (1 Peter 2:5).

hard.q: Why were priests with physical disabilities barred from serving at the altar?
hard.a: Modern readers rightly find this troubling. Several points help put it in context, without removing the difficulty. The rule does not exclude people with disabilities from Israel, from worship, or even from the priesthood: such a priest still ate the most holy food (verse 22). What he could not do was officiate at the altar or approach the veil. Most interpreters understand the restriction as symbolic, parallel to the requirement that sacrificial animals be without blemish: the sanctuary was to display the wholeness and perfection of God's presence, and those who acted in it stood as signs of that. Some scholars add that ancient royal courts expected the same of their servants. Others argue that the rule belongs to a temporary system that pointed beyond itself, and they note that the prophets foresee a day when those once excluded are welcomed (Isaiah 56:3-5, for example, promises eunuchs a place in God's house), and that Jesus healed and welcomed the blind and lame in the temple courts. Christians generally hold that in Christ, the only priest whose perfection matters, these restrictions have been fulfilled, and that disability is no barrier to any service in the church.

questions: The priests were held to higher standards because they stood closer to God's presence. What does this suggest about the responsibility of those who lead in worship or teach today?
The high priest could not show the normal signs of grief even for his parents. What does it cost to serve others while carrying your own sorrow?
Where the priests avoided uncleanness, Jesus touched lepers and the dead. How does his way of holiness challenge the ways you protect yourself from people who seem unclean?
